query: What is the WHO PEN package and what is its purpose?
section: Introduction
ground_truth: The WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions (WHO PEN) for primary care in low-resource settings is a prioritized set of cost-effective interventions that can be delivered to an acceptable quality of care, even in resource-poor settings. It is an innovative and action-oriented response to the challenges of NCD burden in low- and middle-income countries.
hint: Paragraph beginning 'The WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions (WHO PEN)…'

query: What four diseases does the WHO PEN package primarily target?
section: Introduction
ground_truth: WHO PEN targets heart disease, stroke, cardiovascular risk, diabetes, cancer, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The four major NCD groups are cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, and chronic respiratory disease.
hint: Paragraph stating 'WHO PEN is the minimum standard for NCDs to strengthen national capacity to integrate and scale up care of…'

query: What global voluntary targets does WHO PEN aim to help achieve?
section: Introduction — footnotes
ground_truth: WHO PEN aims to help achieve a 25% relative reduction in risk of premature mortality from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease, and prevention of heart attacks and strokes by providing treatment and counselling to at least 50% of eligible people (those with a 10-year cardiovascular risk equal to or above 30%).
hint: Footnote section at the bottom of the Introduction page with two starred bullet points.

query: How does WHO PEN contribute to health system building blocks according to the document?
section: Table ii: Contribution of WHO PEN to Health System Building Blocks
ground_truth: WHO PEN contributes across all six health system building blocks: Leadership/governance (assess needs, support universal coverage), Financing (prioritize NCD interventions for universal coverage), Medical products and technologies (define essential medicines and technologies), Health information system (provide templates for reliable health data), Health workforce (provide training material), and Service delivery (improve access, define cost-effective interventions, improve quality of care and gate-keeper function of primary care).
hint: Table ii on page 10 with six building block rows.

query: What is Protocol 1 of WHO PEN about?
section: WHO PEN Protocol 1
ground_truth: WHO PEN Protocol 1 covers the Prevention of Heart Attacks, Strokes and Kidney Disease through Integrated Management of Diabetes and Hypertension.
hint: Title of Protocol 1 on page 14.

query: What daily salt intake does WHO PEN Protocol 2 recommend?
section: WHO PEN Protocol 2 — Health Education and Counseling
ground_truth: WHO PEN Protocol 2 recommends restricting salt (sodium chloride) to less than 5 grams (1 teaspoon) per day, and advises reducing salt when cooking and limiting processed and fast foods.
hint: Under the 'Eat a heart healthy diet' section, the Salt subsection.

query: What are the recommended fruit and vegetable intake guidelines in Protocol 2?
section: WHO PEN Protocol 2 — Health Education and Counseling
ground_truth: Protocol 2 recommends 5 servings (400-500 grams) of fruits and vegetables per day. One serving is equivalent to 1 orange, apple, mango, banana or 3 tablespoons of cooked vegetables.
hint: Under 'Fruits and vegetables' in Protocol 2.

query: What is the '5 A's' tobacco cessation framework described in Protocol 2, and what happens at each step?
section: WHO PEN Protocol 2 — Tobacco cessation flowchart
ground_truth: The 5 A's framework is: A1-ASK (if patient uses tobacco), A2-ADVISE (to quit in a clear, strong and personalized manner), A3-ASSESS (willingness to make a quit attempt), A4-ASSIST (prepare a quitting plan including set quit date, inform family/friends, remove cigarettes), and A5-ARRANGE (follow-up visit to congratulate success or address relapse). If patient is not willing to quit, the approach shifts to promoting motivation and providing information on health hazards.
hint: Flowchart on page 19 showing the tobacco cessation 5 A's pathway.

query: What clinical features distinguish asthma from COPD according to Protocol 3?
section: WHO PEN Protocol 3 — Diagnosis
ground_truth: Features favouring asthma include: previous diagnosis of asthma, symptoms since childhood or early adulthood, history of hayfever/eczema/allergies, intermittent symptoms with asymptomatic periods, symptoms worse at night or early morning, symptoms triggered by respiratory infection/exercise/weather/stress, and symptoms responding to salbutamol. Features favouring COPD include: previous diagnosis of COPD, history of heavy smoking (>20 cigarettes/day for >15 years), history of heavy and prolonged exposure to burning fossil fuels in enclosed space or occupational dust, symptoms starting in middle age (after 40), symptoms worsening slowly over a long period, and long history of daily cough and sputum production.
hint: Diagnostic comparison table in Protocol 3 with two columns.

query: What is the primary objective of the cancer referral guidelines?
section: Guidelines for referral of suspected breast and cervical cancer — Executive Summary
ground_truth: The primary objective is to guide primary care practitioners in the early identification of patients with signs and symptoms suspicious of breast and cervical cancer so they can be immediately referred to the next level of care for diagnosis and subsequent treatment, if cancer is confirmed.
hint: Second paragraph of Executive Summary for cancer referral guidelines.

query: What age-specific referral criteria exist for women with breast lumps?
section: Cancer referral guidelines — Breast cancer recommendations
ground_truth: Women aged 30 years and older with a breast lump, spontaneous unilateral nipple discharge (particularly bloody), skin changes such as eczematous changes, skin tethering, and skin or nipple retraction should be referred for further investigations. Women under 30 with a breast lump should only be referred if the lump enlarges or has features associated with cancer (fixed or hardness, skin changes) or there are other reasons for concern such as family history of breast cancer, former breast cancer, or prior therapeutic chest irradiation.
hint: Age-stratified bullet points under Breast cancer section.

query: What symptoms warrant speculum examination and immediate referral versus follow-up for cervical cancer?
section: Cancer referral guidelines — Cervical cancer recommendations
ground_truth: Women reporting abnormal vaginal bleeding, persistent foul-smelling discharge, or pain during vaginal intercourse should undergo speculum examination. If a cervical growth or ulceration is found, immediate referral is warranted without manipulation due to significant bleeding risk. If no cervical growth or ulceration is detected, the condition is likely non-malignant (especially in women under 30), and the woman should be treated appropriately and referred to a specialist only if the condition persists or worsens at follow-up.
hint: Two sub-bullet points under cervical cancer describing scenarios with and without cervical growth.

query: Why does the Guideline Development Group provide distinct recommendations by age group for breast and cervical cancer, and what is the specific risk threshold?
section: Cancer referral guidelines — Executive Summary
ground_truth: Women aged 30 years and older have the highest risk of developing breast or cervical cancer, whereas these cancer types are comparatively rare in women under this age. The GDG decided to provide distinct recommendations by age group to ensure focus on women at risk, because otherwise there would be a danger of a dramatic increase of false positives from women under 30 with unnecessary overload of the health system.
hint: Paragraph beginning 'Women aged 30 years and older have the highest risk…'

query: What is the relationship between the cancer referral guidelines and the WHO Comprehensive Cervical Cancer Control guide (C4GEP)?
section: Cancer referral guidelines — Introduction
ground_truth: The referral guidelines target detection of invasive cervical cancer in early clinical stages and are complementary to C4GEP's objectives. C4GEP states that organized population-based screening of women over 30 is the key strategy to reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality. However, where screening is not yet available or is in initial stages, prompt referral based on symptoms and signs is the only other method of diagnosing cervical cancer in earlier stages. Even in well-established screening programmes, some women will present with invasive cancer detectable through warning signs — mainly women who do not attend screening, or who have false negative results or develop interval cancers.
hint: Paragraph beginning 'In the case of cervical cancer, the guidelines target…' in the Introduction.

query: What survival rate differences exist between early-detected and late-stage breast and cervical cancers in low-resource settings?
section: Cancer referral guidelines — Introduction
ground_truth: In low-resource settings, more than 80% of breast and cervical cancers are diagnosed in locally advanced stages or with distant metastases, with a 5-year survival rate ranging between 10-40%. In contrast, the 5-year survival rate for early, localized breast and cervical cancers exceeds 80% in settings where basic treatment is available and accessible.
hint: Paragraph stating 'In low-resource settings, more than 80% of breast and cervical cancers…'

query: What is the stepwise approach to stable asthma management recommended by the guidelines?
section: Recommendations — Management of stable asthma, REC 3
ground_truth: The 5-step approach is: Step 1 — inhaled salbutamol as required (prn); Step 2 — continue salbutamol prn and add inhaled beclometasone 100ug or 200ug twice daily (100ug once/twice daily for children); Step 3 — continue salbutamol prn and increase beclometasone to 200ug-400ug twice daily; Step 4 — add low-dose oral theophylline (assuming long-acting beta agonists are unavailable), or increase inhaled beclometasone dose; Step 5 — add oral prednisolone in the lowest possible dose to control symptoms. At each step, check adherence and inhaler technique.
hint: Numbered steps under REC 3 in the stable asthma section.

query: Why is intravenous aminophylline NOT recommended for routine use in asthma exacerbations, and what is the exception?
section: Recommendations — Management of exacerbation of asthma, REC 7
ground_truth: Intravenous aminophylline is NOT recommended for routine use as a second-line drug because when taken in addition to beta agonists and steroids there is no significant benefit for adults and only marginal benefit for children, while there is evidence of adverse effects for both. The risks outweigh the benefits in settings where monitoring of blood drug levels is not feasible. However, it may be worth trying if available when the patient has not responded to standard treatment and is at risk of dying from asthma.
hint: REC 7 in exacerbation of asthma section, cross-reference with the simplified summary on page 83.

query: What medications are explicitly NOT recommended for stable COPD management and why?
section: Recommendations — Management of stable COPD, RECs 3-5
ground_truth: Three medications are NOT recommended for stable COPD: (1) Oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) — ineffective except possibly in high doses where important side effects occur; (2) Inhaled steroids (beclometasone) — high doses have only a small benefit but more adverse effects including pneumonia, risks unknown in areas with high HIV/TB prevalence, and are expensive for resource-poor countries; (3) Ipratropium bromide — only small benefits compared to regular short-acting beta agonists, more expensive, and no data to assess risk versus benefits of long-term regular use.
hint: RECs 3, 4, and 5 under stable COPD management, all marked as negative recommendations.

query: What is the recommended management for COPD exacerbations?
section: Recommendations — Management of exacerbation of COPD
ground_truth: Management includes: antibiotics for all exacerbations with evidence of infection; oral prednisolone 30-40mg for around seven days for severe exacerbations; high doses of inhaled salbutamol by nebulizer or MDI with spacer; and oxygen if available by a mask limiting concentration to 24% or 28%. Intravenous aminophylline is NOT recommended for routine use.
hint: COPD exacerbation section with 5 recommendations including one negative.

query: Why is oxygen concentration limited to 24-28% for COPD exacerbations but not similarly restricted for asthma?
section: Recommendations — Management of exacerbation of COPD, REC 4
ground_truth: For COPD exacerbations, oxygen should be given by a mask that limits concentration to 24% or 28% (controlled oxygen therapy). This is because COPD patients may have chronic CO2 retention and high-flow oxygen can suppress their hypoxic respiratory drive. In contrast, for acute severe asthma (page 60, REC 3), oxygen should simply be administered without concentration limits, as asthma patients do not have the same risk of suppressed respiratory drive from oxygen administration.
hint: Compare REC 4 of COPD exacerbation (page 62) with REC 3 of asthma exacerbation (page 60).

query: What are the WHO diagnostic criteria for diabetes based on fasting plasma glucose?
section: Recommendations and evidence — A. Diagnosing diabetes
ground_truth: Diabetes is diagnosed with fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/l (126 mg/dl) or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl). Impaired Glucose Tolerance (IGT) is fasting plasma glucose <7.0 mmol/l and 2-hour plasma glucose ≥7.8 and <11.1 mmol/l. Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) is fasting plasma glucose 6.1-6.9 mmol/l.
hint: Table 2 on page 98 showing diagnostic criteria.

query: Can point-of-care glucose devices be used for diagnosing diabetes, and what is the evidence?
section: Recommendations and evidence — Diagnosing diabetes
ground_truth: Point-of-care devices can be used for diagnosing diabetes if laboratory services are not available (strong recommendation, ungraded evidence). Results show good agreement with laboratory methods on the same sample, but analytical accuracy varies across professional standards. The epidemiological studies were not suitable to determine sensitivity and specificity because none compared blood glucose values obtained by two methods in the same blood sample, so a GRADE table was not produced.
hint: Recommendation 1 under the point-of-care question and surrounding evidence discussion.

query: What is the evidence basis for recommending metformin as first-line therapy, and what are its contraindications?
section: Recommendations and evidence — B. Glycaemic control — Metformin
ground_truth: Metformin is recommended as first-line oral hypoglycaemic agent (very low quality evidence, strong recommendation) for patients not controlled by diet who do not have renal insufficiency, liver disease or hypoxia. Evidence comes from a Cochrane review of RCTs. In UKPDS 34, metformin patients had significantly lower risk of any diabetes-related death and macro/microvascular outcomes (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.60-0.90) and all-cause mortality (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49-0.93). Regarding lactic acidosis, a Cochrane review provides high quality evidence that the risk is low and not higher than with other hypoglycaemic agents. Metformin should be discontinued during acute severe illness and the patient referred.
hint: Pages 101-103, spanning the metformin recommendation, UKPDS results, and lactic acidosis discussion.

query: How do metformin and sulfonylureas compare in terms of glycaemic control, mortality outcomes, and hypoglycaemia risk?
section: Recommendations and evidence — B. Glycaemic control — Sulfonylureas
ground_truth: Metformin and sulfonylureas perform similarly in lowering HbA1c (high quality evidence from 17 trials). Five RCTs reported on all-cause mortality with a small effect favouring metformin (low quality evidence). Two RCTs on cardiovascular outcomes did not favour either drug (low quality evidence). Critically, there is high quality evidence from nine RCTs that the risk of hypoglycaemia is higher with sulfonylureas than with metformin. Therefore sulfonylureas are recommended only for patients with contraindications to metformin or in whom metformin does not improve glycaemic control.
hint: Pages 103-104 comparing the two drug classes across outcomes.

query: What blood pressure targets are recommended for diabetic patients and what drugs are first-line?
section: Recommendations — Diabetes guidelines
ground_truth: The target diastolic blood pressure is ≤80 mmHg (moderate quality evidence, strong recommendation) and target systolic blood pressure is <130 mmHg (low quality evidence, weak recommendation). Low-dose thiazides (12.5 mg hydrochlorothiazide or equivalent) or ACE inhibitors are recommended as first-line treatment and can be combined. Beta blockers are NOT recommended for initial management of hypertension in diabetic patients but can be used if thiazides or ACE inhibitors are unavailable or contraindicated.
hint: Blood pressure-related bullet points in the diabetes recommendations summary.

query: What evidence supports giving statins to all diabetic patients aged 40 and over, and what are the contraindications?
section: Recommendations and evidence — C. Reducing CVD risk — Statins
ground_truth: A meta-analysis of 76 randomized trials found statins have beneficial effects on all-cause mortality, revascularisation, risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, with relatively mild adverse events (conditional recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Statins' therapeutic effect comes largely from lowering LDL cholesterol with possible lipid-independent beneficial effects on blood vessels. Regarding contraindications, lovastatin and simvastatin are contraindicated in HIV positive patients receiving protease inhibitors or ritonavir. Despite generic availability, cost could still limit implementation in low-resource settings.
hint: Pages 105-106, statin recommendation with evidence and Table 3 footnote on HIV contraindications.

query: What specific foot care and retinopathy screening recommendations exist for diabetic patients?
section: Recommendations — Diabetes guidelines
ground_truth: For foot care: patients should receive health education on foot hygiene, nail cutting, treatment of calluses, and appropriate footwear (low quality evidence, strong recommendation). Health care workers should be educated on assessment of feet at risk of ulcers using simple methods — inspection and pin-prick sensation (low quality evidence, strong recommendation). For retinopathy: persons with type 2 diabetes should be screened by an ophthalmologist when diabetes is diagnosed and every two years thereafter, or as recommended by the ophthalmologist (low quality evidence, conditional recommendation).
hint: Final set of diabetes recommendations regarding feet and eyes.

query: What are the emergency management protocols for hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia in diabetic patients?
section: Recommendations — Diabetes guidelines — Emergencies
ground_truth: For severe hypoglycaemia (unconscious patients on hypoglycaemic agents and/or blood glucose ≤2.8 mmol/L): administer intravenously 20-50ml of 50% glucose (dextrose) over 1-3 minutes; if unavailable, substitute with any hypertonic glucose solution; provide food as soon as the patient can ingest safely (very low quality evidence, strong recommendation). For hyperglycaemia (blood glucose ≥18 mmol): refer to hospital with IV drip of 0.9% NaCl, 1 litre in 2 hours, continue at 1 litre every 4 hours until hospital (very low quality evidence, strong recommendation).
hint: Last two bullet points of the diabetes recommendations on page 89.

query: What is the purpose of the WHO/ISH cardiovascular risk prediction charts?
section: Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease — Assessing cardiovascular risk
ground_truth: The WHO/ISH risk prediction charts indicate 10-year risk of a fatal or non-fatal major cardiovascular event (myocardial infarction or stroke), according to age, sex, blood pressure, smoking status, total blood cholesterol and presence or absence of diabetes mellitus for 14 WHO epidemiological sub-regions. They help identify those at high cardiovascular risk and motivate patients to change behaviour and, when appropriate, take antihypertensive, lipid-lowering drugs and aspirin.
hint: Instructions for using WHO/ISH risk prediction charts section.

query: What six data inputs are needed to use the WHO/ISH cardiovascular risk charts?
section: Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease — How to use the charts
ground_truth: The six inputs needed are: (1) presence or absence of diabetes, (2) gender, (3) smoker or non-smoker status (all current smokers and those who quit less than 1 year before assessment are considered smokers), (4) age, (5) systolic blood pressure (mean of two readings on each of two occasions), and (6) total blood cholesterol (mean of two non-fasting measurements by dry chemistry, or one non-fasting laboratory measurement).
hint: Bulleted list under 'Before applying the chart…' with footnotes 6-9.

query: Under what conditions can drug therapy decisions be made before formally grading cardiovascular risk using the charts?
section: Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease — Primary prevention
ground_truth: Drug therapy can be initiated before grading cardiovascular risk in people with: established cardiovascular disease; total cholesterol ≥8 mmol/l (320 mg/dl) or LDL cholesterol ≥6 mmol/l (240 mg/dl) or TC/HDL-C ratio >8; persistent raised blood pressure >160-170/100-105 mmHg; type 1 or 2 diabetes with overt nephropathy or other significant renal disease; and renal failure or renal impairment. All of these individuals need intensive lifestyle interventions and appropriate drug therapy regardless of their chart-derived risk score.
hint: Bulleted list under 'When can the decision be made to give drugs even before grading the cardiovascular risk?'

query: What factors can make the actual cardiovascular risk higher than indicated by the WHO/ISH charts?
section: Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease — Practice points
ground_truth: CVD risk may be higher than indicated when the patient is: already on antihypertensive therapy, has premature menopause, is approaching the next age/SBP category, has obesity (including central obesity), is sedentary, has family history of premature CHD or stroke in first degree relative (male <55, female <65), has raised triglycerides (>2.0 mmol/l or 180 mg/dl), has low HDL cholesterol (<1 mmol/l or 40 mg/dl in males, <1.3 mmol/l or 50 mg/dl in females), has raised CRP/fibrinogen/homocysteine/apolipoprotein B/Lp(a)/fasting glycaemia/impaired glucose tolerance, has microalbuminuria, has raised pulse rate, or experiences socioeconomic deprivation.
hint: Practice points section listing conditions where 'CVD risk may be higher than indicated by the charts.'

query: What equipment and drugs are needed to implement cardiovascular risk assessment at primary care level?
section: Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease — Resource needs
ground_truth: Equipment needed: stethoscope, accurate blood pressure measurement device, measuring tape and weighing scale, equipment for testing urine glucose and urine albumin, and assay of blood glucose and blood cholesterol. Drugs needed: thiazide diuretics, beta blockers, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, aspirin, metformin, insulin, statins. Other facilities: system for maintaining medical records and referral facilities. Human resources: medical doctor or trained nurse/non-physician health worker.
hint: Resource needs section with bulleted categories.

query: How does the document define self-care?
section: Self-care — Executive Summary
ground_truth: Self-care is defined as 'the ability of individuals, families and communities to promote health, prevent disease, and maintain health and to cope with illness and disability with or without the support of a healthcare provider.' It involves the entire body of health decisions individuals make for themselves and their families, including staying fit, avoiding hazards like smoking, self-monitoring, self-management, self-medication, and improved management of long-term conditions.
hint: Quoted definition at the beginning of the Executive Summary for Section III.

query: Why did the guideline development group find it difficult to make strong recommendations either for or against most self-care interventions?
section: Self-care — Executive Summary
ground_truth: Many self-care interventions are enthusiastically advocated by policymakers, health workers, educational systems and NGOs, and have wide appeal. However, very few are based on high or moderate quality evidence of effectiveness, making strong recommendations in their favour inappropriate. On the other hand, there is similarly a lack of high or moderate quality evidence of no effectiveness, accompanied by considerable uncertainty over harms outweighing benefits, making strong recommendations against their use also inappropriate given their popularity and intuitive appeal.
hint: Paragraph beginning 'Many of the self-care interventions in NCDs identified in the 9 questions…'

query: What are the nine self-care research questions addressed by the guideline, and what methodological approach was used?
section: Self-care — Questions
ground_truth: The nine questions address whether the following improve outcomes in NCD patients: (1) community/support network strategies, (2) lay-led self-management programmes, (3) online resources, (4) self-monitoring devices, (5) mobile telephone/telemonitoring interventions, (6) self-treatment interventions, (7) self-care education/information programmes, (8) self-care rehabilitation programmes, and (9) interventions targeted at adherence. The methodology used systematic reviews rated with the AMSTAR tool, with a search for clinical trials specifically from LMIC, and the GRADE approach for quality of evidence and strength of recommendations.
hint: Pages 132-133 listing all nine questions with definitions, and the methodology paragraph on page 131.

query: What is the recommendation regarding lay-led self-management programmes for NCDs in LMIC?
section: Self-care — Recommendations table, Question 2
ground_truth: The use of highly structured lay-led self-management patient programmes for self-care in NCDs is not recommended at the present time for LMIC (weak recommendation, very low quality evidence). Research is needed to evaluate lay-led self-management programmes in LMIC, ideally with identification of the active components and their feasibility in low-resource settings.
hint: Recommendation 2.1 in the self-care recommendations table.

query: What is the definition of self-treatment intervention and how does it differ from self-monitoring?
section: Self-care — Questions, Question 6
ground_truth: Self-treatment intervention includes self-monitoring AND adjustment of dosage of medicines by the individual based on a pre-specified action plan agreed jointly by a health care practitioner and the patient. This differs from self-monitoring alone (Question 4), which involves monitoring a biochemical or physical measure (e.g. blood pressure, blood glucose, peak flow) in the home or community setting with results communicated to a health professional for ongoing management. Self-treatment adds the element of autonomous medication adjustment under professional guidance.
hint: Compare the definitions given for Questions 4 and 6 on pages 132-133.

query: What is the estimated total cost of implementing best buy NCD interventions across all low- and middle-income countries?
section: Scaling up action against NCDs — Summary
ground_truth: The average yearly cost for all low- and middle-income countries is estimated to be US$ 11.4 billion, with an overall cost of US$ 170 billion over the period 2011-2025.
hint: Summary section stating 'The average yearly cost for all low- and middle-income countries…'

query: What is the per-capita cost of implementing the NCD best buy package by country income level?
section: Scaling up action against NCDs — Summary
ground_truth: The annual investment per head of population is: under US$ 1 in low-income countries, US$ 1.50 in lower middle-income countries, and US$ 3 in upper middle-income countries. As a proportion of current health spending, this amounts to 4% in low-income countries, 2% in lower middle-income countries, and less than 1% in upper middle-income countries.
hint: Two sentences after the total cost figure giving per-capita and percentage breakdowns.

query: What are the five core parameters used in the NCD costing tool to estimate scale-up costs, and how do they interact?
section: Scaling up action — Methods — Costing principles
ground_truth: The five parameters are: (1) population of the country/region, (2) prevalence/incidence of the disease or risk factor, (3) coverage — proportion of population in need receiving the intervention, (4) resource quantities needed to implement the intervention (human resources, medicines, equipment), and (5) prices or unit costs for each resource item. Population times prevalence defines the population at risk/in need; resource use times price provides cost per case; and coverage is the main mechanism by which scale-up takes place over time.
hint: Bulleted list on page 176 and the paragraph explaining how the parameters interact.

query: What distinguishes a 'best buy' intervention from a 'good buy' intervention according to the costing methodology?
section: Scaling up action — Methods — Selection of interventions
ground_truth: A 'best buy' extends beyond economic efficiency or cost-effectiveness: it is an intervention with compelling evidence for cost-effectiveness that is also feasible, low-cost and appropriate to implement within the constraints of the local health system. A 'good buy' is an intervention that does not meet all of these criteria but offers good value and has other attributes that recommend its use. Policy-makers should consider best buys as a core set for priority scale-up, and good buys as an expanded set to be made available when resources allow.
hint: Paragraph defining 'A best buy is a concept that extends beyond economic efficiency…'

query: How many countries were included in the costing analysis, what was the selection criteria, and how were total costs extrapolated?
section: Scaling up action — Methods — Scale-up period and country selection
ground_truth: Analysis was carried out for 42 low- and middle-income countries, each with more than 20 million people, accounting for 90% of the NCD burden in developing regions and 77% of the global NCD burden. They were grouped as: 13 low-income, 13 lower middle-income, and 16 upper middle-income countries. Total costs for all low- and middle-income countries were approximated by multiplying results for the 42 countries by a factor of 1.11 (100%/90%), since they account for 90% of the population in developing regions.
hint: Table 2 showing country lists and the paragraph explaining the 1.11 multiplication factor.

query: What default coverage rates were assumed for current and target intervention coverage in the costing model?
section: Scaling up action — Methods — Coverage levels and scale-up patterns
ground_truth: For most best buy individual interventions in primary care, a default current coverage rate of 5% was adopted. The target coverage level was set at 80% for 2025. The exception is hepatitis B immunization, where country-specific data show high coverage already — in 33 of the 42 countries, coverage exceeds 80%, so additional expenditures are only needed in countries below this level. For tobacco control, the world's population covered by demand reduction measures was below 10% in 2008.
hint: Paragraphs under 'Coverage levels and scale-up patterns' discussing default rates and exceptions.

query: What population-based best buy interventions are included for addressing NCD risk factors?
section: Scaling up action — Table 1 Summary of interventions
ground_truth: Population-based best buy interventions include: for tobacco use — tax increases, smoke-free indoor workplaces and public places, health information and warnings, bans on advertising and promotion; for harmful alcohol use — tax increases on alcoholic beverages, comprehensive restrictions and bans on marketing, restrictions on retail availability; for unhealthy diet and physical inactivity — salt reduction through mass media campaigns and reduced salt in processed foods, replacement of trans-fats with polyunsaturated fats, and public awareness programmes about diet and physical activity.
hint: Table 1 upper section listing population-based interventions.

query: What methodology was used across the different guideline sections and how was evidence quality assessed?
section: Diabetes guidelines — Methodology and process
ground_truth: The guidelines used the GRADE methodology to formulate relevant questions and identify important outcomes. Databases searched included Medline/PubMed, Embase, DARE, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews up to December 2010. Systematic reviews were considered suitable if up-to-date in 2008 or later and scored 8 or more on the 11-point AMSTAR tool. The GRADE approach classified evidence quality as high, moderate, low or very low, and recommendation strength as strong or weak — reflecting confidence that benefits outweigh harms and the intervention's relevance to LMIC in terms of feasibility and resource implications.
hint: Methodology section of diabetes guidelines cross-referenced with the self-care methodology on page 131.

query: What measurements should all people aged 40+ years have according to the diabetes guideline development group?
section: Recommendations and evidence — A. Diagnosing diabetes
ground_truth: The guideline development group agreed that all people 40+ years should have: waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting or random plasma glucose, urine protein, urine ketones in newly diagnosed diabetes, plasma cholesterol if the test is available, and testing of foot pulses and sensation if known to have diabetes.
hint: Paragraph after the diagnostic criteria table beginning 'The guideline development group agreed…'

query: What specific complications does WHO PEN aim to prevent through its integrated NCD management approach?
section: Introduction — Why do we need these implementation tools?
ground_truth: WHO PEN aims to prevent heart attacks, stroke, kidney failure, amputations, and blindness through early detection and management of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, chronic respiratory diseases and cancer. It also targets reduction of premature mortality and prevention of complications through integration of NCD care into primary health care using cost-effective interventions.
hint: Second bullet point under 'Why do we need these implementation tools?'

query: What are the key distinctions between financial and economic costing, and total versus incremental costing in the NCD costing tool?
section: Scaling up action — Methods — Box 1 Costing principles
ground_truth: Financial vs economic costing: costs reflect actual expenditures from a health-system perspective; travel costs of patients/families and economic-value costs (travel time, lost productivity) are excluded. Total vs incremental costing: total cost calculates costs for the entire population in need at specified coverage, unadjusted for existing expenditures; incremental costing assumes current spending continues and only includes resources/expenditures required above current levels. The tool also separately estimates variable costs (treatment costs dependent on patient numbers) and fixed capital costs (equipment, buildings) that do not vary per patient.
hint: Box 1 on page 175 with definitions of three costing distinction pairs.

query: What evidence exists for the glycaemic control threshold and its relationship to microvascular complications?
section: Recommendations and evidence — B. Glycaemic control
ground_truth: Studies comparing intensive versus less intensive glycaemic control showed no glycaemic control threshold effect for complications. However, patients achieving HbA1c values of 7% or below had significantly lower risk of microvascular complications than less intensively treated patients with higher mean HbA1c (7.9-9.4%). An HbA1c of approximately 7% corresponds to fasting plasma glucose of approximately 6.5 mmol/l. The ADVANCE trial found major microvascular outcomes (new or worsening retinopathy or nephropathy) reduced by 14% in the intensive group. The UKPDS found 25% relative risk reduction in aggregate microvascular endpoints.
hint: Paragraph spanning the DCCT, ADVANCE, VADT and UKPDS evidence discussion on pages 99-101.

query: A 45-year-old heavy smoker presents at a primary care clinic with persistent cough, worsening breathlessness, a blood pressure reading of 165/100 mmHg, and fasting blood glucose of 7.2 mmol/L. He also reports he cannot stop smoking. According to WHO PEN, what combination of protocols applies to this patient, what diagnostic steps should be taken to distinguish his respiratory condition, what cardiovascular risk threshold determines whether he needs drug treatment, and what is the step-by-step approach to help him quit tobacco?
section: Multi-protocol — Protocol 1 + Protocol 2 + Protocol 3
ground_truth: This patient requires three WHO PEN protocols: Protocol 1 (CVD/diabetes/hypertension), Protocol 2 (lifestyle counselling and tobacco cessation), and Protocol 3 (respiratory disease). For respiratory diagnosis: features favouring COPD over asthma include heavy smoking (>20 cigarettes/day for >15 years), symptoms starting in middle age, persistent daily cough and sputum, and worsening breathlessness with little day-to-day variation. For cardiovascular risk: drug treatment is indicated when blood pressure is ≥160/100 mmHg or when 10-year cardiovascular risk is ≥30%; this patient's BP of 165/100 meets the threshold. For tobacco cessation, the 5 A's apply: A1-ASK (confirm tobacco use), A2-ADVISE (quit clearly and strongly), A3-ASSESS (willingness to quit), A4-ASSIST (set quit date, inform family, remove cigarettes), A5-ARRANGE (follow-up to congratulate success or address relapse). Since the patient cannot stop, motivational counselling and health hazard information should also be provided.
